candidates.attacker_control: Any authenticated user with an OAuth2 access token for their own account controls: the target path segment (`/Users/{ownId}`), the `If-Match` header (`*` is accepted by `getVersion`), and the full JSON body, including `origin`, `externalId`, `verified`, `active`, `userName` and `email`. No privileged scope is required because the `@self.isUserSelf(request,1)` expression is an alternative to `scim.write`.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Considered that UAA intentionally permits self-service profile updates: the existing guard class shows which fields the codebase itself treats as non-self-modifiable (email, username, verified, active, origin), and the snapshot wires that guard nowhere (searched whole tree for 'ScimUserSelfUpdateAllowed' and 'selfUpdateAllowed': only the class file matches). Considered that deactivation might invalidate tokens: UaaTokenServices.loadAuthentication (lines 776-840) rebuilds the authentication from the token and user id with no active/verified/locked check, and no salt/token revocation is performed on deactivation in ScimUserEndpoints.deleteUser. Considered that `ScimUtils.validate` might constrain values: it only enforces a username pattern when origin is `uaa` and exactly one email - it does not prevent origin/active/verified changes. Considered server-side scoping: `IdentityZoneHolder` scopes the record to the current zone, but the attacker's own record is in that zone, so it does not mitigate.
candidates.impact: Authorization-control bypass and account-integrity compromise: a user can undo administrative deactivation, self-verify an unverified account, and convert an externally managed (LDAP/SAML/OIDC) account into a locally managed `uaa`-origin account with a self-set password - bypassing SSO/IdP controls and preserving stale local group/scope memberships (LDAP group synchronization only happens on LDAP logins). Changing `userName`/`email` also enables identity/profile manipulation on the record.
candidates.prerequisites: A valid bearer token for the user's own UAA record (ordinary user token). For self-reactivation: the account must have been deactivated by an administrator but the previously issued access token must still be within its validity window (UaaTokenServices.loadAuthentication does not check the user's active/verified/locked state). For the SSO-bypass variant: the attacker must control the email address stored on their external-IDP-provisioned record so the reset mail reaches them.
candidates.root_cause: The `/Users/**` filter chain authorizes PUT/PATCH for the caller's own user with `@self.isUserSelf(request,1)` only; no field-level restriction is applied. `ScimUserEndpoints.updateUser`/`patchUser` pass the caller-supplied object to `JdbcScimUserProvisioning.update`, whose SQL writes `origin`, `verified`, `externalId`, `userName`, `email`, `active` (and salt). The codebase contains an unused guard, `ScimUserSelfUpdateAllowed.isAllowed(request)`, which compares the database record against the request body and returns false when email, username, verified, active or origin differ - exactly the missing check. Additionally `ScimUser.patch()` copies `active`/`verified` unconditionally from a patch object whose primitive defaults are both `true`, so even a PATCH body that omits those fields forces them to true. `ScimUserEndpoints.updateUser` also calls `checkIsEditAllowed(user.getOrigin(), request)` with the attacker-supplied body origin rather than the stored origin, so the disable-internal-user-management guard is evaluated against attacker-chosen data.
candidates.title: Self-service SCIM update of a user's own record allows changing security-sensitive attributes (origin, active, verified, externalId, username, email)
candidates.trace: 1) User obtains a normal access token (e.g. via LDAP/SSO login or password grant). 2) `PUT /Users/{self}` with `If-Match: *` and a JSON body containing e.g. `"origin":"uaa"`, `"active":true`, `"verified":true` (or `PATCH` with any body, since `ScimUser.patch` sets active/verified from defaults). 3) scim-endpoints.xml line 231/232 allows the request because `@self.isUserSelf(request,1)` is true. 4) `ScimUserEndpoints.updateUser` (263-284) / `patchUser` (286-311) forwards the object without field filtering; only `ScimUserSelfUpdateAllowed` (unused) would have rejected the origin/active/verified change. 5) `JdbcScimUserProvisioning.update` (238-276) writes the attacker-chosen `origin`/`active`/`verified` values. 6) With `origin=uaa`, the public `/forgot_password` flow (`UaaResetPasswordService.forgotPassword`, line 153, queries `userName ... and origin eq "uaa"`) issues a reset code to the attacker-controlled email, letting the attacker set a local password and log in through the internal user store, bypassing the external IdP. In the reactivation case the account is active again despite administrative deactivation.
candidates.unverified: No code execution or runtime verification was possible: the snapshot contains no tests, and the mail/reset chain (forgot-password -> emailed code -> local password) was traced by source reading only, not executed. Exact behavior of a deactivated account's previously issued token is inferred from the absence of an active-state check in UaaTokenServices.loadAuthentication, not observed at runtime. Whether upstream UAA considers some of these field changes (e.g. verified) acceptable for self-update is a design question the snapshot cannot fully settle; the unused guard class is the strongest signal that these fields were meant to be immutable for self-updates.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization / CWE-284 Improper Access Control (missing field-level authorization on a self-service object update)

coverage_summary: Coverage is limited to the 1,186 text source files exposed by the snapshot filters (binary-like files skipped; no symlinks or sensitive-name exclusions reported by get_source_scope). Test sources are entirely absent (@@src/test@@ contains 0 files), so verification relied on production code, Spring XML security configuration, and Thymeleaf templates. I read the SCIM user/group endpoints and provisioning, client-admin and identity-zone endpoints, OAuth authorization/token/refresh/revocation classes, JWT signature/validation utilities, LDAP/Keystone/SAML/OIDC authentication managers and configuration classes, password-reset/change-email/invitation flows, the security filters (CORS, CSRF, session, zone-switching), redirect handlers, guard/utility classes, and the relevant Spring XML filter chains (scim-endpoints, oauth-endpoints, login-server-security, multitenant-endpoints, identity-zones, saml-providers). I did not read every one of the 1,186 files line-by-line; dependency-level CVEs (Spring Security OAuth 2.3.0, Spring 4.3.20, etc.) were out of scope because external lookups are not permitted.
limitations: No runtime execution, test execution, or exploit payloads were used (per instructions); all conclusions are source-level and unconfirmed.
The repository snapshot omits all test sources, so the guard classes'/expected behaviors could not be cross-checked against tests that may exist upstream.
The snapshot exposes only the assigned tree; upstream history/fix commits and sibling versions were not available, so I could not diff against the fixed version to identify the exact intended patch.

Several findings require deployment assumptions (which identity providers are configured, whether logout whitelists are restrictive, whether the JDK/browser URL parser normalization applies) that cannot be validated inside this run.
SAML/OIDC signature-verification and LDAP-binding code was reviewed only at a high level; deeper cryptographic verification paths were not exhaustively audited.

rejected_leads.lead: Logout redirect control is inert: `Links.Logout.isDisableRedirectParameter()` returns a constant false and `setDisableRedirectParameter(boolean)` ignores its argument (model/src/main/java/org/cloudfoundry/identity/uaa/zone/Links.java lines 64-70), while `ZoneAwareWhitelistLogoutHandler` (lines 51-55) feeds this value into `setAlwaysUseDefaultTargetUrl`. `WhitelistLogoutHandler.isAlwaysUseDefaultTargetUrl()` (lines 33-36) also returns false, so the `logout.redirect.parameter.disable` option cannot take effect.
rejected_leads.reason: Blatant control defect, but I could not establish a concrete, unauthenticated open redirect from it: `WhitelistLogoutHandler.determineTargetUrl` still passes the target through `findMatchingRedirectUri(whitelist+clientURIs, target, defaultTargetUrl)` with the non-null default `/login`, so non-whitelisted external URLs fall back to /login. Classified as a security-control/hardening defect rather than the primary memory-corruption-free vulnerability; kept as a secondary lead because it is clearly defective code.

rejected_leads.lead: Open-redirect/parser-differential in `UaaUrlUtils.uriHasMatchingHost` (server/src/main/java/org/cloudfoundry/identity/uaa/util/UaaUrlUtils.java lines 231-242) used by `UaaSavedRequestCache` (line 95) and `UaaSavedRequestAwareAuthenticationSuccessHandler` (line 42) for `form_redirect_uri`: `new URL(uri).getHost()` can differ from what the browser navigates to for authorities containing a backslash before '@' (e.g. `https://evil.com\@uaa-host`).
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible but depends on JDK URL parsing versus browser WHATWG normalization, which cannot be verified with the read-only, no-execution tools available; impact is an open redirect of a post-login redirect parameter rather than token/credential compromise.

rejected_leads.lead: `UaaUrlUtils.findMatchingRedirectUri` documents and implements an open redirect when the whitelist is empty and the fallback is null (lines 92-114), used by `EmailChangeEmailService.completeVerification` (line 127) where the client's `change_email_redirect_url` may be null, and by `SamlRedirectLogoutHandler`/`WhitelistLogoutHandler`.
rejected_leads.reason: Reaching the unfiltered redirect requires a valid emailed expiring code (sent to the new email address), so the redirect is attacker-influenced mainly for the attacker's own flow; the login-page path re-checks the host via `uriHasMatchingHost`. Impact too limited and conditions too strong to be the primary candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: SCIM `patch()` overwrites `active`/`verified` with model defaults `true` unconditionally (model/src/main/java/org/cloudfoundry/identity/uaa/scim/ScimUser.java lines 327-329 and 770-775), enabling self-reactivation of a deactivated user via PATCH.
rejected_leads.reason: Kept as part of the main candidate's trace rather than a separate candidate because it is another manifestation of the same self-service update path; on its own it is one root-cause facet, not a distinct issue.

rejected_leads.lead: `UaaRequestMatcher.matches` uses a prefix (`startsWith`) match on the request URI (server/src/main/java/org/cloudfoundry/identity/uaa/security/web/UaaRequestMatcher.java line 108), and `AccessController.getLocation`/`InvitationsController` build absolute URLs from the `Host` header (AccessController lines 285-287; InvitationsController lines 168-172).
rejected_leads.reason: Prefix matching is hardening-relevant only if a distinct controller is mapped under a path with the same prefix; Host-header injection requires the ability to make the victim's browser send a forged Host (proxy/misconfiguration), which is not demonstrated by source evidence alone.

summary: Reviewed the UAA 4.28.0-SNAPSHOT source tree (1,186 model/server/module files; tests are absent from the snapshot). The strongest evidenced issue is in the SCIM user API: self-service updates (`PUT`/`PATCH /Users/{self}`) are authorized solely by `@self.isUserSelf(request,1)` in the security configuration, while neither the controller nor the JDBC provisioning layer restricts which fields may change. The record body (deserialized by `ScimUserJsonDeserializer`) can carry `origin`, `externalId`, `verified`, `active`, `userName` and `email`; `JdbcScimUserProvisioning.update` persists all of them. A purpose-built guard class (`ScimUserSelfUpdateAllowed`) that exists precisely to reject self-updates changing email, username, verified, active or origin is present but is not referenced by any configuration or production code, confirming both intent and the missing enforcement. Concrete impact: a deactivated or externally-managed (LDAP/SAML/OIDC) user holding a still-valid token can reactivate their own account, self-verify, or convert their record to `origin=uaa` and then obtain a local password through the self-service reset flow, bypassing the external identity provider/SSO controls. Several other leads (logout redirect flag, redirect-host checks) were examined and rejected as weaker/unconfirmed and are noted below.
